title: Composite pattern: treat trees and single objects the same, TypeScript example — cv.cm
description: The Composite design pattern explained: build tree structures where leaves and groups share one interface. TypeScript file-system example and real uses.
answer: Composite is a structural design pattern that lets you compose objects into tree structures and then treat individual objects and groups of objects in the same way. A leaf (such as a file) and a composite (such as a folder that contains files and other folders) implement the same interface, for example `size()`. The composite implements the operation by calling it on its children, so client code can work with a whole tree without checking what kind of node it has.

body: Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly. It is one of the seven structural patterns in the Gang of Four (GoF) book.

Imagine a storage app that must show the total size of any item. A file has a size. A folder's size is the sum of everything inside it, and a folder can contain files and other folders, nested to any depth.

Without a common interface, every piece of code that walks the tree must ask "is this a file or a folder?" and handle each case, usually with recursion written again and again. Adding a new node type, such as a shortcut or a compressed archive, means finding and updating every one of those checks. Composite puts the recursion inside the nodes themselves.

Type-safe: you cannot add a child to a file. But clients must know when they hold a composite.
`Component` declares `add()` and `remove()`, and leaves throw or ignore them.

body: In TypeScript, the safety approach usually works better, because the type checker catches the mistake at compile time.

body.note: Recursion in a composite can be expensive on large trees. In the example, `print()` calls `size()` at every folder, which walks the subtree again. For big trees, cache results or compute sizes in one pass. Also make sure a node cannot be added to its own subtree, which would create infinite recursion.

sections.h: When to use it, and when not to

ul: Your data is naturally a tree: files and folders, UI widgets inside containers, menus and submenus, organization charts, drawing shapes and groups.
Clients should be able to ignore the difference between one object and a group of objects.
The structure is flat or always one level deep. A plain array is simpler.
Leaves and groups need very different operations. Forcing them into one interface creates methods that make no sense for some nodes.
You need to restrict which children a composite may hold, for example only certain node types. The uniform interface makes such rules harder to enforce in the type system.

The DOM: every element and text node is a `Node`. Elements can contain other nodes, and many operations, such as `textContent` or `cloneNode(true)`, work the same on a single node and on a whole subtree.
UI component frameworks such as React, Vue and Angular build interfaces as trees where a component can render other components.
Java AWT and Swing: `Container` is a subclass of `Component` and holds other components, so a panel full of buttons is itself a component.
Abstract syntax trees in compilers, scene graphs in game engines, and nested menus all follow the same idea.
Iterator: traverses the nodes of a composite without exposing how children are stored.
Visitor: adds new operations over a composite tree (export, validation, statistics) without changing the node classes.
Decorator: also has a component interface and wraps objects recursively, but a decorator has exactly one child and adds behavior, while a composite has many children and combines their results.
Builder: is often used to construct complex composite trees step by step.
Chain of Responsibility: often uses the parent links of a composite, passing a request up from a child to its parents, as browser events bubble up the DOM.

faq.q: What is the difference between a leaf and a composite?
faq.a: A leaf has no children and does the work itself. A composite holds child components and usually does its work by calling the same operation on each child and combining the results.
It is designed for tree-shaped part-whole hierarchies. A general graph with cycles needs extra care, such as tracking visited nodes, to avoid infinite recursion.

faq.q: What is the difference between Composite and Decorator?
faq.a: Both use a shared interface and recursive composition. A decorator wraps exactly one object to add behavior, while a composite groups many children to treat them as one.

faq.q: Should add() be on the leaf class too?
faq.a: Only if you want full transparency and accept run-time errors when someone adds a child to a leaf. In typed languages it is usually safer to put `add()` on the composite only.
